learning_objective: 🎯 Understand the purest form of motion (1D kinematics). Learn the difference between speed and velocity, and master the three equations of motion!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Path length (Distance) is the total actual distance covered (a scalar). Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from start to finish with a specific direction (a vector). Displacement can be zero, but distance cannot!

Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time. Instantaneous velocity is how fast you are going at one EXACT moment (like looking at your car's speedometer). In calculus, it's the derivative of position: $v = dx/dt$.
Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. If you speed up, slow down (deceleration), or change direction, you are accelerating! Formula: $a = dv/dt$.
For uniform (constant) acceleration, we have three magic equations: 1. $v = u + at$ 2. $x = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ 3. $v^2 = u^2 + 2ax$. They only work if 'a' is constant!
On a Position-Time (x-t) graph, the slope gives Velocity. On a Velocity-Time (v-t) graph, the slope gives Acceleration, and the area exactly under the curve gives the Displacement!

fun_activity.title: 🍏 The Gravity Drop
fun_activity.instructions: Hold a heavy book and a crumpled piece of paper at the exact same height and drop them simultaneously. They hit the ground at the same time! This proves Galileo's law: in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the exact same acceleration ($g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$).

exam_tips: 📌 Always define your sign convention. Generally, take upwards as positive ($+y$) and downwards as negative ($-y$). In free fall, acceleration is always $a = -g$.
📌 'Stopping distance' of a vehicle is a common 2-mark derivation. Formula: $d_s = -u^2 / 2a$.
📌 If a particle reverses direction, distance and displacement will differ. Always split the motion at the point where velocity becomes zero!
quick_recap: ⭐ Speed is always positive, but velocity can be positive, negative, or zero depending on the direction.
⭐ The area under an acceleration-time (a-t) graph gives the change in velocity.
⭐ Free-fall is the classic example of motion under uniform acceleration.
